"Papa, can I go on that one?" Arohi pointed at the tallest slide in the water park, the one that looped.
"You're nine. That's for grown-ups," Ujjwal said.

I'm Leela and I'm ten. Last summer at my Nani's village I nearly died of boredom. There was nothing new. Same mango tree, same well, same cows.
So I made up games. I tried climbing to the top branch of the mango tree. I tried jumping over the stream at its widest point. My cousin Rehana said I was mad.
"Why can't you just sit and play carrom?"
"Carrom is boring! I want to feel my heart go boom!"
When I fell in the stream, Nani pulled me out and said, "At least tell me before your next adventure." So I did. The next one was riding the bullock cart with the farmer, holding the rope, with Nani waving.
Best day of the whole summer.

qa.a: At Nani's village.

qa.a: Nani didn't ban it, but asked Leela to tell her first, so Leela could have thrills with an adult knowing and nearby.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Leela's adventures?
qa.a: Rehana thinks Leela is mad and prefers calm games like carrom.

grounding: A child finds the familiar boring and seeks thrills like climbing and jumping, feeling excitement is life itself.

I'm Parul. In Class 6, I was the girl who never broke a rule. I tucked in my shirt, wore my hair in two plaits like everyone, and said "Good morning, Ma'am" in the same voice as the others.
One day in science, Ma'am said plants eat soil. I knew from a book that that's not quite right. My hand went halfway up, then came down. What if everyone laughed? What if Ma'am was cross?
My friend Jomon asked me at lunch, "Why didn't you say it? You told me yesterday."
I shrugged. "I didn't want to make trouble."
But I felt small all afternoon. Being good kept everyone happy. It also kept me quiet.

qa.q: What did Ma'am say plants eat?
qa.a: Ma'am said plants eat soil.

qa.q: What was Parul afraid of when her hand came down?
qa.a: She was afraid everyone would laugh or that Ma'am would be cross, so she felt nervous about speaking up.

qa.q: What could Parul try next time she knows something different?
qa.a: She could ask a polite question, like 'I read something else, can I share?', or speak to Ma'am after class.

qa.q: How does Jomon see Parul's silence?
qa.a: Jomon is puzzled, since Parul had shared the answer the day before, and seems to wish Parul had spoken.

grounding: A child follows every rule and fits in with dress and speech, fearing disapproval, and buries her own opinion.

Yusuf is the most well-behaved child in class. He always has his tie straight, his homework done and his voice low. He copies the words and jokes the popular boys use, even when they don't seem to fit him.
During group work, Lakshmi suggested a wrong answer. I saw Yusuf frown, write something else, and then rub it out and agree with her. Afterward I asked him privately. He said, "I didn't want her to be upset with me, Ma'am."
I told him that his ideas matter, and that kind disagreement is allowed. Next week I'll give him a role as group reporter, so he practises sharing his view.

qa.a: By telling him his ideas matter and kind disagreement is allowed, and giving him the role of group reporter to practise.
